Este vocabulario aparece en el manual de: This vocabulary appears in the manual of any device you use. The padlock on a web page is a cipher; the barcode and the QR are encodings, and they protect nothing; the invisible watermark on a banknote is steganography. And when an application asks you for a password “of at least 12 characters”, it is asking for the key space to be large: with letters, digits and symbols there are about 95 symbols per position, and $95^{12}$ is a 24-digit number. With 6 characters, $95^6$ has 12, and a graphics card gets through it in an afternoon.

Alice wants to send a message to Bob, and Eve listens to everything that passes through the channel. Eve cannot be stopped from listening: the channel is a letter passing through many hands, a radio wave, an internet cable. What can be done is to make what she hears useless to her. To that, and only that, cryptography is devoted.

Auguste Kerckhoffs, a Dutch linguist settled in Paris, published in 1883 La Cryptographie Militaire with six requirements for a cipher; the second, that the system should not require secrecy and could fall into the enemy's hands without harm, is the one that bears his name. Parece natural pensar que un sistema es: It seems natural to think a system is safer if nobody knows how it works. History says the opposite, over and over. A method is shared with many people, written down in manuals, built into machines that get captured; sooner or later it becomes known. In 1883 Auguste Kerckhoffs put it in writing: a system has to remain secure even if everything but the key falls into the enemy's hands. Tres cosas que se confunden y que convie: Three things that get confused and are worth separating from day one. Encoding is changing a message's form with a table everybody knows: Morse, computers' ASCII, braille. It hides nothing; it only adapts it to a medium. Hiding is Eve not even knowing there is a message: invisible ink, a text inside a photograph. It is steganography, and it fails as soon as somebody looks properly. Encrypting is transforming the message so that even someone who has the whole of it cannot read it, unless they know a small, secret piece of data: the key.
